q: An 81-year-old woman taking methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis develops cytopenia and oral mucosal ulcerations. Which mechanism is listed for this drug in Hazzard's treatment table?
o: Inhibition of the enzyme dihydrofolic acid reductase
Inhibition of the cellular synthesis of pyrimidines
Neutralization of the cytokine TNF by an antibody
Blockade of the receptor for the cytokine IL-1
explanation:
Methotrexate is a folate antagonist. **Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase** helps explain toxicity in rapidly dividing marrow and oral mucosa.

**A. Inhibition of the enzyme dihydrofolic acid reductase.** Less reduced folate is available for DNA synthesis. Cytopenias and mouth ulcers fit this effect.
**B. Inhibition of the cellular synthesis of pyrimidines.** Inhibition of de novo pyrimidine synthesis is characteristic of leflunomide.
**C. Neutralization of the cytokine TNF by an antibody.** Neutralization of TNF is the action of biologics such as adalimumab.
**D. Blockade of the receptor for the cytokine IL-1.** Anakinra blocks IL-1 receptor signaling.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1614.

q: מה הטיפול שאינו מומלץ ליובש בעיניים במטופל הסובל ממחלת SJOGREN?
o: טיפות Pilocarpine
אנטי TNF
Cyclosporine
Silicone Implants.לצינור הדמעות
explanation:
Sjögren disease reduces tear production and can inflame the ocular surface. Local treatment replaces or retains tears and controls inflammation. **TNF inhibition is not recommended to treat Sjögren-related dry eyes.**

**A. Pilocarpine drops.** Pilocarpine can stimulate residual gland secretion. The usual Sjögren secretagogue is oral pilocarpine. The eye-drop formulation should not be mistaken for routine dry-eye treatment.
**B. Anti-TNF treatment.** Etanercept and infliximab have not shown meaningful clinical benefit for primary Sjögren disease.
**C. Topical cyclosporine.** It can reduce ocular-surface inflammation in selected patients with persistent symptoms.
**D. Silicone punctal plugs.** Occluding tear outflow can retain the tears a patient still produces.

Reference · British Society for Rheumatology guideline on management of adult and juvenile onset Sjögren disease, 2025, pp. 419–422, 424.

q: Before using the rheumatoid-arthritis classification score in Hazzard Table 101-1, which clinical entry conditions must be met?
o: Joint pain may replace clinical synovitis when rheumatoid factor is positive
Clinical synovitis qualifies even when another disease explains it better
Positive anti-CCP antibodies qualify even without any clinical joint synovitis
Definite clinical synovitis must be present without a better alternative explanation
explanation:
The RA classification score estimates the likelihood of rheumatoid arthritis in a patient with **clinical synovitis in at least one joint that another diagnosis does not explain better**.

**A. Joint pain may replace clinical synovitis when rheumatoid factor is positive.** Pain alone can occur without synovial inflammation. Positive rheumatoid factor cannot replace a swollen joint.
**B. Clinical synovitis qualifies even when another disease explains it better.** A more convincing diagnosis, such as crystal arthritis, must be considered before applying the score.
**C. Positive anti-CCP antibodies qualify even without any clinical joint synovitis.** Anti-CCP contributes points after the patient meets the clinical entry conditions.
**D. Definite clinical synovitis must be present without a better alternative explanation.** Definite synovitis and the absence of a better explanation are both required before counting joints or scoring serology.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1608.

q: How useful is anti-CCP antibody testing for distinguishing LORA from polymyalgia rheumatica?
o: One small study found the same positivity in LORA, PMR and healthy older controls
One small study found positivity in 65% of PMR but none of LORA or healthy controls
One small study found positivity in every LORA patient and none of the PMR patients
One small study found positivity in 65% of LORA but none of PMR or healthy controls
explanation:
Late-onset rheumatoid arthritis can resemble polymyalgia rheumatica through shoulder pain and stiffness. **Anti-CCP positivity favored RA** in this small comparison.

**A. One small study found the same positivity in LORA, PMR and healthy older controls.** Identical positivity would not distinguish the groups. Antibodies were detected only in the RA group.
**B. One small study found positivity in 65% of PMR but none of LORA or healthy controls.** The 65% figure belongs to late-onset RA. The PMR group had no positive results.
**C. One small study found positivity in every LORA patient and none of the PMR patients.** Sensitivity was incomplete. About one-third of the patients with RA tested negative.
**D. One small study found positivity in 65% of LORA but none of PMR or healthy controls.** Positivity in 65% of the RA group and none of the PMR or control groups makes a positive result informative. A negative result cannot exclude RA.

Reference · Hazzard 8e Ch 101 - p1611

q: What RA-specific risk requires evaluation before intubating a patient with long-standing disease?
o: Protection of the cervical spine by long-standing RA
Overextension as a means to prevent spinal-cord compromise
Absence of cervical risk after more than 10 years of RA
Cervical spine disease and atlantoaxial joint instability
explanation:
Rheumatoid synovitis can damage the upper cervical joints and their stabilizing ligaments. **Assess for atlantoaxial instability before manipulating the neck for intubation.**

**A. Protection of the cervical spine by long-standing RA.** Long-standing inflammation increases susceptibility to instability.
**B. Overextension as a means to prevent spinal-cord compromise.** Overextension can endanger the spinal cord or brainstem if the upper cervical vertebrae are unstable.
**C. Absence of cervical risk after more than 10 years of RA.** A long disease duration raises concern even when neck symptoms are limited.
**D. Cervical spine disease and atlantoaxial joint instability.** Recognizing cervical instability changes airway positioning and the intubation plan.

Reference · Hazzard 8e Ch 101 - p1612

q: Which interpretation best explains the association between Sjögren syndrome and lymphoma described in Hazzard?
o: Chronic T-cell stimulation drives the predominantly T-cell malignant transformation.
Loss of autoantibodies signals restoration of the normal antibody-producing population.
A monoclonal IgM spike reflects resolution of the benign exocrine process.
Chronic B-cell stimulation drives progression from benign exocrinopathy toward lymphoma.
explanation:
Sjögren syndrome causes autoimmune inflammation of exocrine glands, particularly the salivary and lacrimal glands. **Persistent B-cell stimulation** is a proposed explanation for how a reactive glandular infiltrate can give rise to a malignant B-cell clone.

**A. T-cell transformation.** T cells participate in glandular inflammation, but the lymphomas associated with Sjögren syndrome arise predominantly from B cells.
**B. Loss of autoantibodies.** Autoantibody levels can fall when lymphoma cells displace normal antibody-producing plasma cells. Falling levels can therefore accompany progression.
**C. Monoclonal IgM signals recovery.** A new monoclonal IgM band indicates production by one clone and may herald lymphoma. It warrants evaluation.
**D. Chronic B-cell stimulation.** Persistent glandular lymphoid proliferation can pass through a reactive stage called pseudolymphoma before a malignant clone emerges.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1626.

explanation:
Late-onset rheumatoid arthritis can begin abruptly with synovitis in a few large or proximal joints. **Rheumatoid nodules are often absent** in this presentation.

**A. Absent rheumatoid nodules.** Nodules are an extra-articular manifestation. An older patient can have active rheumatoid synovitis without palpable nodules.
**B. Slow onset over years.** New joint swelling can be the first manifestation. Several years of gradually progressive symptoms are unnecessary for this diagnosis.
**C. Predominant small hand-joint involvement.** Small joints can be involved, but shoulders and other large joints are especially characteristic at onset in older adults.
**D. At most three joints.** Two or three inflamed joints would fit. The late-onset pattern described includes two to six joints, so three is too restrictive as an upper limit.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1610, Table 101-2.
